#4099. Holiday Gaming With Kids And Family

Ahead of the holiday season, we gathered some of our favorite video game recommendations focused on family interaction, spoke with Jackbox Games and Halfbrick (creators of Bluey’s Quest for the Gold Pen) about what it takes to make a game that everyone can enjoy together, and even have tips for new parent gamers hoping to introduce kids to their (and our) favorite hobby.

From its inception, video games were created to encourage social interaction. Tennis for Two in 1958, arguably the first video game, had two players compete in digital tennis against one another. The single-player video game came later, and as much as we love them, some of our best gaming memories are centered around playing with family and friends. And as we get older, we’re making new gaming memories with our own kids.

Making video games is hard. That any game crosses the finish line is a miracle of teamwork and perseverance, and the hardest trick of all is making the final product feel effortless. Arguably, none are more practiced at feeling like effortless joy machines than the games that effectively include players of all ages and skill levels in the experience. And to take it a step further, Jackbox Games is perhaps the best at this sub-genre of video games: inclusive party games that are genuinely for everyone.

Jackbox Games studio creative director Arnie Niekamp sheepishly and humbly agrees when I offer this accolade and also says thank you. “It really matters to us,” Niekamp says. “We really value, first, just inclusivity in general, and are always trying to think of how we can make our games playable by as many people as possible, or how we can expand that.”

Jackbox Games has released its 12th Party Pack by the time you’re reading this issue, and part of the secret of that ongoing success is that its creators stick with the company for a long time. “The person that came in and started making games as a young single person also ages into having a family, having kids, and having that perspective of, ‘Oh wait, it’s also really fun to play these games with my kids, with my family.’”

Even if a game is primarily focused towards young players, being fun for everyone is “very important” Halfbrick writer Brendan Deboy says when talking about making Bluey’s Quest for the Gold Pen. “Bluey’s humor, relationships and themes give children and parents reasons to enjoy its stories together. We wanted that shared enjoyment to carry into the game.”

Brooke Breit, Jackbox’s game product manager and The Jackbox Party Pack 12’s lead, cites that family element as an important detail to making games for everyone. “We playtest our games constantly throughout production amongst ourselves, and that’s one of the markers of, ‘Are we hitting success within the mechanics? Within how it plays?’” Breit says. “And part of that also involves us playing with our own families as a part of that playtesting process [...] All of our kids have a lot of opinions on what makes a really good Jackbox game.”

Breit also points out a metric the team has accidentally discovered over the years that has helped them figure out why a game works for all ages when the creation process happens to be going well. “There’s a little bit of… maybe the younger and older crowd also intersects with the drunk crowd,” Breit says with a thoughtful laugh.

Deboy also discusses the importance of family playtesting saying, “Children of Halfbrick parents playtested the game, with ages ranging from four to 10. Their parents reported what they enjoyed most and where they became stuck.” And avoiding the stickiness is crucial. “We wanted challenges to be satisfying without any single obstacle preventing someone from seeing the rest of the game,” Deboy says. “If something is too difficult, they can leave it, try another activity and return later. Harder challenges were often tucked away in harder-to-find places, helping players encounter easier activities first.”

Jackbox also figured out another secret weapon for great family gaming and gaming with kids: getting away from cell phones. This may be an odd element to cite considering the vast majority of Jackbox games are played collectively on individual phones, but when you’re using your phone as a controller, you’re not using it to check social media.

“You can’t get phones out of people’s hands anyway, so you might as well use it as a tool,” Niekamp says. “Engagement is absolutely a huge part of our design, and we talk a lot about what is on your device,” Breit says. “What is on the game screen? Where do we want people’s focus to be at any given moment? And are we giving opportunity and motivation for people to talk to each other and actually engage with each other?”

Deboy cites another way to encourage engagement as it did with Halfbrick’s Bluey game. “We wanted everyone to be able to finish the game, while giving players of different ages and abilities things to enjoy. That meant providing choices. Some activities test timing and motor skills, while others reward exploration, searching or logical thinking. Players can choose what suits them without having to complete every obstacle.”

When asked what other cooperative and family-focused games are doing right and wrong, Deboy and the Halfbrick team recalled games they played (and got annoyed with) when they were young. “Some of us remembered childhood games where one difficult boss or tricky section stopped us from ever reaching the end,” Deboy says. “You could spend weekend after weekend trying, or replay the opening levels because those were the only ones you could finish. That experience informed our approach.”

Niekamp points out his appreciation for games like Mario Party (which he calls brilliant, but wishes it moved a little faster), but mainly says there just aren’t enough fun co-op family games. “I wish there were more,” Niekamp says. “Especially when your kids are younger, there’s a real sweet spot of like… it’s so great when you start playing stuff together, and finding those things is so incredible and awesome, and then you just start to feel like you run through them pretty fast, and you’re sort of looking for more.”

We agree with Niekamp, and alongside helpful tips for how to introduce young or new players to video games, you can also read on for some of our recommendations (including a different, but similarly fun Bluey video game) for recent games we think are particularly suited to playing with your family.

Whether it’s your friend’s kids, nephews and nieces, or your own children, many of us are eventually confronted with the challenge: How can I share my love of gaming with someone younger who is just getting into the hobby, and enjoy the experience with them? Here are some tried-and-true tips that have served us well.

Especially with the youngest set, gaming can start with opportunities to watch and contribute as you play. Choose low-complexity exploration games with some freeform choices about where to go, cozy games with building options, or age-appropriate narrative games. You handle the controls, but let your kid choose how to proceed. Talk to them about what you’re doing. Tell them more about the game and why you like it. Help them feel like the cool things that happen are the result of their choices.

It should perhaps go without saying, but once they have their hands on the controller, accept moving slowly as a rule. Encourage small wins like learning which button does what. Don’t criticize mistakes. Acknowledge that losing and failing, and then coming back to try again, is part of the fun. Choose games with simple control inputs, easy modes, and forgiving restarts on failures. If you want them to eventually be able to play at your level, be patient enough that they want to keep playing.

Once they’re ready to actively play together, it’s hard to go wrong with cooperative play. In particular, watch for titles that allow one cooperative partner to help the other out of a bind with revives, carries, or boosts. Celebrate together when you overcome a notable challenge, even if you did most of the work.

Start with short sessions, and follow their interests and focus level. Even if you’re in the middle of an exciting section of a game, take a break when you sense they’re getting frustrated – at least at first. Regardless, don’t play too long. Resilience in confronting really tough encounters, puzzles, or challenges can come with time. Watch for things that are scary – even if they don’t seem like they should be scary – and either divert from that thing, or talk together about the difference between a game and real life.

There are plenty of amazing online games, and many can be safe to play with kids. But other players add a level of randomness that can lead to major frustration, unsafe incoming communication, and wildly different skill levels. Start with games that don’t require playing with others online, and if you do graduate to online play at some point, stay directly involved in play sessions.

While you can introduce your favorites, kids will quickly learn what they like. Follow that enthusiasm, and engage with the games and experiences they’re excited about. Ignore the advice above that doesn’t apply to your new gamer; some kids will love competitive play or be eager to confront high challenge and frustration, and that’s just fine. Like most things about raising kids – listen to what they’re communicating, and build what they love into your gaming together.

Good family games have the potential to become memorable staples in bonding and communication. Here are some recent games we’d recommend for playing together with the people you love and the people who annoy you (but you still love them anyway).

Parents likely need no introduction to the Heeler family; the anthropomorphic dogs are nearly ubiquitous in popular culture. Thankfully, Bluey and friends’ newest video game is a welcome treat, offering stress-free, simple gameplay you can enjoy solo or with a partner. Bluey finds an old Polaroid-style camera and sets out to scrapbook, snapping pictures of all sorts of animals, games, and friends as she explores sites like the Park and Riverbank, often unlocking additional stickers and decorations for her new hobby. Like the show, Happy Snaps is charming and often funny, and its sandbox-style exploration hints at a refreshing curiosity about the world. - Matt Miller

Some games can be fun multiplayer experiences even if they weren’t intended to be. Solving dense puzzles in Blue Prince or Lorelai and the Laser Eyes as a group is fun, but if you’re mixing in younger players, grab The Mermaid Mask. Captain Magnus Mortuga was murdered aboard his submarine, and the killer is still loose; you’re tasked with gathering testimony, analyzing evidence, and solving bizarre puzzles. Charming animations and voice performances make this a great fit for family, so long as they’re old enough to handle cartoon bloodstains and themes of mortality. - Charles Harte

The loot-driven action of the Diablo franchise is a potent mix of multiplayer and RPG mechanics that just about any fan of video games can appreciate. But its violence and tone mean it’s not one you necessarily want to play with younger adventurers. Minecraft Dungeons and its recently released sequel, however, offer the same fun RPG growth trajectory and accessible combat without all that pesky blood. The game also offers local multiplayer for up to four players, which means it’s very easy for the family to get together and play in a world the kids are likely already very familiar with. - Kyle Hilliard

Released on Switch in 2023 and ported to Switch 2 with myriad added bells and whistles in 2026, Super Mario Bros. Wonder expertly toes the line between new and old. Fans of Mario’s NES roots can enjoy the plumber’s latest adventure and experience some of the best 2D platforming the medium offers, and new players get to learn what makes the world of Mario so charming. With multiple playable characters, local co-op play, and lots of options to try different abilities, Wonder is a great introduction to Mario and also just a great game. - Kyle Hilliard

Disney Illusion Island is an all-ages adventure that can double as your child’s first-ever platformer and a family co-op session centered around the joy of movement in games. Play as Disney’s iconic Fab Four – Mickey, Minnie, Donald, and Goofy – as you explore the various biomes of the mythical Monoth while trying to save its inhabitants. There’s no combat, so even your littlest ones can enjoy the fun of exploring these beautifully hand-drawn 2D spaces, and hilarious cutscenes will have everyone on the couch laughing. Three free DLCs will keep the adventure going after credits, too. - Wesley Leblanc

When it comes to playing a video game with family of any age – young, old, or in the middle – you really can’t go wrong with a Jackbox game. There is some reading required, but if you know how to use a phone, then you can participate, and you will enjoy yourself. 12 includes a game about sorting trivia questions into the right categories at high speed, one where you try to make the most ridiculous greeting card, a game encouraging silly debates, one that identifies connections among everyone playing, and finally Hyperface, where you manipulate selfies. Just make sure to toggle on the “family-friendly” option in the settings to omit some of the more adult jokes and prompts. - Kyle Hilliard

Everyone remembers the excitement of Wii Sports back in 2006. That game, with its fun selection of tech-demo sports minigames, permeated pop culture and reached a mainstream audience in ways few other games can claim. Nintendo Switch Sports Resort may not have the same cultural impact as Wii Sports, but it’s a superbly fun and approachable collection of sports-based minigames. Whether you want to reignite your love for virtual bowling and archery or cruise around Wuhu Island on land, sea, or air, Nintendo Switch Sports Resort is an enjoyable experience that’s simple to pick up and play for gamers of all ages and experience levels. Read our full review. - Brian Shea

Convincing kids to do a family activity isn’t always an easy task, but saying the words, “You can play as Spider-Man,” makes it a whole lot smoother. Marvel Cosmic Invasion is a beat ’em up reminiscent of arcade classics from the ’90s, but with modern controls and conveniences. Kids will have fun with favorites like Iron Man, Captain America, and Black Panther, while older superhero fans will appreciate inclusions like Phyla-Vell and Beta Ray Bill. With approachable controls, vibrant pixel art, and an electric soundtrack, it makes for a super Saturday morning experience. - Charles Harte

Since the world of Pokémon debuted in Japan in 1996 on the Game Boy, it has evolved to become a cross-generational staple for nostalgic adults and young players eager to learn about and pick their favorite creature. Pokopia is arguably the best Pokémon game in years and is a much more relaxing affair than the games that revolve around combat. Progress requires some reading, and it’s worth noting that the multiplayer options are limited, complicated, and require multiple Switch 2 consoles. But as a fun pass-the-controller way to work together and build a new world for all your Pokémon experience, it is an undeniable success. - Kyle Hilliard

Mario Party is admittedly the king of the board game-style genre it popularized (and 2024’s Super Mario Party Jamboree is a great option in that regard), but Lego Party is a genuine contender for the genre crown. The Lego of it all offers more flexibility in terms of theming for worlds and minigames. Players also vote on the minigames they want to play, and winning awards more than just currency – it also affects subsequent turn order, which makes it all feel a little more rewarding. The consistent commentary is also genuinely funny and helps keep everyone engaged while others take their turns. - Kyle Hilliard

There are some games that are just known to be great for families that, frankly, you probably don’t even need to be reminded of. There is a reason millions play Fortnite every day; Mario Kart, Mario Party, and Smash Bros. are among Nintendo’s best-selling games of all time, and it’s so easy to get lost in a Minecraft world of your own creation. These games are family staples, but just in case you weren’t already familiar, you should probably check them out.

#4098. Zenless Zone Zero Version 2.7 brings Angels of Delusion to the battlefield with playable Nangong Yu

Champions Never Fall to the Past indeed, as Zenless Zone Zero prepares for a major update that fans of Angels of Delusion will appreciate.

HoYoverse has delivered another Special Program for the second day running, this time for Zenless Zone Zero. The developer revealed the full details of Version 2.7, subtitled Champions Never Fall to the Past.

This next major update arrives March 24, adding two new Agents, and introducing the Hollow Champion competition.

Most things in Version 2.7 follow on from the Hollow Champion competition, which brings together old friends and familiar faces, as well interesting newcomers. Everyone is in it to win some big rewards and earn glory.

Among the unexpected participants the competition has attracted are the Public Security's Metropolitan Order Division, and even some former Calydon's Sweepers. A big challenge that awaits is Black Wolf Romeul, who’s capable of increasing his Crit Damage Resistance and Interruption Resistance by activating a Corruptive Barrier.

Romeul can also cause enemies to continuously lose HP, but you can beat him by putting together a squad that can deal sustained Anomaly damage, which will break through the barrier quickly.

Our first new arrival in Version 2.7 is Cissia of the Metropolitan Order Division. She is an S-Rank Electric Attack Agent who automatically gains three stacks of Venom when she enters the battle. Each stack deals Electric Damage while also increasing her Crit Rate for a time.

When she runs out of Venom, which will happen, Cissia can generate more stacks by using her EX Special Attack. She can also use her Basic Attack, Serpent's Kiss, to better utilise the new stacks of Venom she generates.

The other new Agent may be the more exciting. Nangong Yu, the captain and lead dancer of the Angels of Delusion, can now be part of your team. Nangong Yu is an S-Rank Ether Stun Agent who can boost her team’s Anomaly Buildup Rate against Stunned enemies.

Being part of an idol group has its perks, because she automatically regenerates Downbeat as time goes on, and even more any time a squad member inflicts an enemy with Anomaly. Nangong Yu can then use Downbeat - after enough has been accumulated - on charged attacks that keep enemies stunned for longer. Her Ultimate triggers Ether Veil: Delusion Reprise, which boosts the entire squad’s Attack.

Returning Agents in Version 2.7 will be Yidhari, the S-Rank Ice Rupture Agent, as well as Seed, the Electric Attack Agent.

Outside of all the very important action in the core story, this chapter also brings new themed events to Lumina Square’s Simmer Hot Pot Restaurant. The Simulated Battle Trial is also getting some love, with updated mechanics and new enemy line-ups.

Catch up on our recently updated Zenless Zone Zero character tier list, and don’t forget to check out these Zenless Zone Zero codes before you jump in for some free stuff.

#4097. Fans Reject Universes Beyond In New MTG Set Poll From Mark Rosewater

It may be only a small sample of players, but the message is clear: Universes Beyond isn't going to win out over in-universe sets.

There have been a whopping seven Magic: The Gathering sets released this year, and players agree on one thing: it was way too many. Six is the standard figure expected moving forward, with a 50/50 split between in-universe and Universes Beyond.

Over on his Blogatog, Magic's lead designer, Mark Rosewater, held a poll asking players what their favorite set of 2026 was, and while the overall winner was a little predictable, there are still some surprising results, and none look particularly good for Universes Beyond.

In the poll held on his Blogatog, Mark Rosewater listed all seven sets, along with the option for "I refuse to pick one." The final results, which show that 2,695 people voted, indicate that Reality Fracture wins by a landslide at 44.8%, with the next closest set being Secrets of Strixhaven at 15.9%, followed by Lorwyn Eclipsed at 15.1%.

A bit of quick math shows that this already accounts for 75.8% of the total vote, and the next highest entry at 9% is the aforementioned pick refusal, which takes us to 84.8%. This leaves just over 15% spread across the remaining four sets, all of which were Universes Beyond offerings. Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles came in last with 2.2%, followed by The Hobbit at 2.5%, Star Trek at 4.3%, and finally Marvel Super Heroes at 6.3%.

This sample size isn't nearly big enough to represent anything beyond players tuned into Mark Rosewater's blog at the time of the poll, but it's still a scathing indictment of Universes Beyond, and it doesn't help the seemingly growing calls for change following Star Trek's failure.

The Universes Beyond sets are often extremely divisive, but some are much better than others, so we've ranked every one so far.

The biggest sign that Universes Beyond isn't going anywhere anytime soon is that Wizards of the Coast is already planning sets for 2030 and beyond, with the current yearly 50/50 split in mind. This would mean at least nine more Universes Beyond sets planned beyond 2027.

One thing we're starting to see with Universes Beyond is learning between sets. The original Universes Beyond sets that were Standard legal were in the works for so long that we're only now reaching a point where lessons learned from those sets are starting to impact the design of future ones.

Marvel Darkhold Destiny feels like the first set that's truly taking a lot of the fan feedback on board, which is leaning very heavily into adopting Marvel into the world of Magic using a brand new original story and character, rather than just smashing the two properties together and seeing what comes out the other side.

If we look at some of the biggest complaints about Star Trek, then we'd expect the main takeaways to be less reliance on properties that use real-life actors, far less artwork that is just 'character standing and pointing', and not taking mechanics and settings that could make for a great in-universe set (Star Trek could easily have been Edge of Eternities 2, for example) and wasting them on a Universes Beyond property.

Universes Beyond is a part of Magic now, and the best we can hope for is that it improves with each new release, and eventually even the loud minority who oppose it come round to enjoy (or tolerate) its inclusion.

#4096. Feature: Seven Improvements We'd Still Love To See In GTA 6

There's no two ways about it: GTA VI is a blummin' brilliant game, well worthy of its universally acclaimed 99 Metacritic score. But just because we gave it a 10/10 here at Pure Xbox doesn't mean there isn't still some wiggle room for improvement.

Both Fraser and I have put many hours into this enormous RPG already, and have come away floored by its grandeur. However, we've also noticed a few things we'd like to see fixed or added to GTA VI to make it even better. Think of this article like adding marshmallows to a hot chocolate: we're looking to take something great and make it even sweeter.

We've whipped up a few of our own suggestions and mixed in some from across the world wide webbies to bring you our top improvements we'd like to see in GTA VI. Let's get into it:

On this page: Seven Improvements We'd Still Love To See In GTA 6

You've all noticed the darkness that appears from time to time around the screen, right? That's a vignette and GTA VI is a big fan of them. It's most noticeable when you're booking it down the North 97 highway or, in the worst-case scenario, flying over the Keys as shown in the above screenshot.

GTA VI uses vignettes to cleverly draw your focus to the most important parts of the screen. I honestly think it's a great technique for making things feel more cinematic. Although, it is quite pants that there's no option to reduce its intensity or turn it off altogether. If Rockstar could give us the ability to toggle the vignette on and off, that would be great, because it also seems to be one of the most requested changes amongst GTA VI players.

Something I've grown increasingly aware of is the inability to wait or sleep to pass time across Leonida. I was particularly irked after an 18-hole crazy golf competition against Jason saw the sun set on us, and I didn't fancy driving all the way back to my lodging in Vice City. I wanted to pass time in my car or a nearby eatery, but my only option appeared to be the 4-5 minute drive home - made worse knowing that once morning hit, I'd just want to do the drive back and play golf in the daylight.

It's probably the fault of Red Dead Redemption 2 and its extremely handy wilderness camps. They were great in a pinch to let you pass time quickly. What would be great is if GTA VI gave players the option to rough it in their car for the night or find a nearby hotel room or something.

I was on a mission to pick up some prescription drugs when my car was escorted slowly into an enemy compound and the camera suddenly switched from third-person to first-person. Seeing Lucia's impeccable nails gripped around the steering wheel made me realise there's no legitimate way to drive from a behind-the-wheel perspective.

Sure, there's that glitch that lets you play GTA VI in first-person, but it would be better if Rockstar implemented an additional first-person POV for driving.

It seems like a bit of a no-brainer, but we'd love to see AMD FSR 4.1 implementation on Xbox Series X. GTA VI is already up-and-running with FSR 4.1 on Xbox Series S which brings internal resolutions up from 720p to 1080p output. It's good going on XSS, but we'd like to see what it can do with XSX.

If a game launches with a good Photo Mode, then you may as well tack an extra 10 hours onto my playthrough. But GTA VI? Maybe add another 20-30 hours. It's gorgeous!

The Photo Mode in this game is already solid. You can set up light sources, adjust focus and aperture, and as a graduate photographer, I think it's all rather intuitive. There's even a selfie mode where players can pose Jason and Lucia together, adjust their facial expressions and change their poses.

What I'd like to see is that same flexibility expand beyond selfie mode. I'd like to be able to adjust the lovers to better match the photos I'm trying to create. It was during a tense getaway, four-stars and neck-deep in trouble, that I thought I'd take an action shot, only to find Jason had blinked and Lucia looked bored as hell. It would be great to have the option to adjust expressions, head directions, poses and all that sort of stuff.

Please fix the sliders when handling amounts of money, Rockstar. Please. It's not the biggest fix, nor the most elaborate, so I'll keep it brief.

Whenever I open my phone to buck myself some cash, I often struggle to select the right amount quickly. It takes too long for the slider to speed up as I increase the amount, but then it very quickly gets out of control, and I end up overshooting my intended figure. Plus, the sound it makes is quite horrid.

What would help is having set increments to scroll through, say, $1, $10, $50, $100 and so on. It might just smooth out the experience a smidge.

I'd like to wrap up with a quickfire segment of some of our own suggestions on how Rockstar could improve GTA VI, but also some of yours. So, let's get through it.

I'd love to be able to call NPC buddies like Cal for a round of crazy golf. At the moment, playing with a partner is limited to Jason and Lucia. I'm all for love, but sometimes you need some friendly bonding too.

Another one I'd personally like to see is custom music stations on in-game radios. Now, I know this isn't something likely to happen, but it would be cool to link my Spotify and Rockstar accounts to play my own curated playlists.

Oh, and for the love of all things matrimony, please let me make a coffee for Jason/Lucia and actually give it to them. I've experienced Jason asking for a cuppa joe, so let me do the do, y'know?

Something Fraser mentioned he'd like to see is additional minigames like bowling or darts added to the game. The developers said they ran out of time for things like this, so maybe they could add them as a post-launch update.

And to wrap up, I've spotted folks online requesting the ability to dial any phone number like you could in previous games, as well as blind firing around cover during firefights, buying housing property, and having save states pick up directly where you left off.

So, there you have it. Some of our suggestions and some we've found out in the wild, but we'd love to hear your ideas on what might make GTA VI a better game. Be sure to chat with us in the comments!

#4095. Ubisoft Wants Rayman To Become A Huge, Transmedia Star

Ubisoft is gearing up to launch Rayman Legends Retold, a reimagined remake of the 2013 original. While many have questioned the decision to remake a game that arguably still looks and plays great to this day, the developers have been clear in their intention to use Retold as a launchpad for the future of the franchise.

Now, in a new interview with The Game Business, brand producer Loïc Gounon has expressed much broader ambitions for the character, perhaps bringing Rayman more in line with something like Sonic in terms of visibility.

In other words, Gounon is thinking about not only games, but other mediums too, including TV shows and comics. The first step is to ensure the brand's success in regions such as the US and Asia, with previous Rayman titles' success being largely limited to Europe.

“I would like to see Rayman as a must-have IP for video games across the world. Rayman was generally stronger in France and the UK, and in some cases in the US. Enlarging the reach of the IP, also towards Asia and performing well in the US, is the first ambition… making sure that we are a must-have platforming adventure title across those markets in the video game world.

“And I guess beyond the video game world. So, comics, TV series... actually, there’s a French comic book that came out with Rabbids and Rayman being reconnected.”

However, Gounon does not necessarily believe that producing a new 3D title is the key to success, and instead wants to focus on the characters and lore. Sorry to those hoping for Rayman 4 – hey, it might still happen!

“Rayman is iconic because of its gameplay. But going back to the adventure roots of Rayman, having people dive into those characters, exploring deeper into that world and mythology, that’s what we believe in.

“It’s the world-building part, the consistency of that world-building, and the empathy for those characters, that will make the franchise last and maybe become bigger.”

Rayman Legends Retold is right around the corner, scheduled to launch on 3rd December 2026. Meanwhile, Ubisoft itself is currently coming under fire for its heavy focus on generative AI, with a new report revealing that employees are required to justify reasons for not using the technology in new project pitches.

#4094. How Nintendo Recovered After Stumbling In The Streetpass

By the time Nintendo ceased production of the 3DS in September 2020, the company’s last dedicated line of exclusively handheld video game devices had completed one of gaming’s most incredible comebacks. But to come back, you must first fall, and fall the 3DS did soon after it first launched in February 2011: its first month-and-a-half sales numbers came in nearly 400,000 units short of Nintendo’s initial projections of 4 million units sold. Over the next three months, Nintendo sold just an additional 710,000 3DS units worldwide, with only 110,000 purchased in the United States. In response, Nintendo took drastic measures, slashing the 3DS price in America from $250 to $170 just a half-year after the handheld launched.

The move worked: In its first month at its new price, 3DS sales in America rose 260 percent. According to metrics released by Nintendo last year, the 3DS family of devices ended its run at a stunning 76 million units sold, still half of the original DS’s total but far more than other Nintendo platforms like the GameCube (21.7 million), Nintendo 64 (32.9 million), SNES (49.1 million), and even the original NES (61.9 million). The little system that couldn’t eventually proved it could.

One obvious issue with the launch was the games – or lack thereof. Included in the modest North American 3DS launch lineup were just three Nintendo first-party titles: Nintendogs + Cats, Pilotwings Resort, and Steel Diver. Though a Zelda remake, a new Mario platformer, and a new Mario Kart would arrive by year’s end, traditional system-selling franchises were initially nowhere to be found. By the time the bigger games arrived, Nintendo’s three first-party launch titles were placed in the dustbin of history, something Game Informer predicted in its review of Steel Diver, which labeled the game as “destined to become a strange and forgotten footnote in the publisher’s history.”

Every first-party launch title communicates, both intentionally and unintentionally, something about the system upon which it’s launching and the company that created it. Last year, for instance, Mario Kart World evidenced that seamless open-world design and an interest in making buckets of money would remain hallmarks of Nintendo’s Switch 2 era. So, what can these three largely forgotten launch games tell us about the 3DS and Nintendo more broadly?

Initial hardware reviews of the 3DS contained two recurring thoughts: The glasses-free 3D effect was impressive when it worked – but it didn’t always work. Engadget’s review further hypothesized that “a lot of people are going to buy a 3DS and find they don’t really care for the 3D effect.” By the time Super Mario 3D Land released nine months after launch, Game Informer’s Bryan Vore was startled to find he was using the system’s primary feature at all, writing, “What surprises me most about 3D Land is how well the 3D effect is handled. I kept the 3D slider up most of the game”.

Indeed, in Nintendo’s 2011 fiscal year report, president Satoru Iwata theorized that initial 3DS sales were underwhelming because the company had not done a convincing enough job of explaining the system’s signature innovation to potential customers: “The value of 3D images without the need for special glasses is hard to be understood through the existing media. However, we have found that people cannot feel it just by trying out a device, rather, some might even misestimate it when experiencing the images in an improper fashion.” Just two and a half years after the system’s launch, Nintendo began selling a fully flattened version of the handheld, appropriately named the 2DS.

Part of the issue with the underwhelming launch was that the 3DS lineup lacked an obvious killer app: There was neither a clear game that made purchasing the handheld an easy decision, nor was there a game that immediately proved that the 3D effect was anything more than an optional gimmick. In fact, among the three first-party titles was a game that had been designed nearly to completion before the team even learned of the existence of the 3DS.

When Nintendo first began showing the original DS to journalists at E3 in 2004, included among upcoming releases, like Metroid Prime Hunters and WarioWare Touched!, was a humble submarine simulation tech demo. IGN’s hands-on preview called the sub demo “simple in concept, but surprisingly complex in its controls and gameplay,” noting that it was “one of those ‘fun, but not quite a full game’ games at Nintendo’s booth, so it’s hard to say if development teams will expand on Submarine’s design to make it a more complete package.” At first, the team that made the demo, comprising veterans from Star Fox and F-Zero, was also unsure if they would expand it into a full game, as many of its members began work on other projects like Wii Fit.

Much later, producer Tadashi Sugiyama said in an Iwata Asks interview posted on Nintendo’s website that Nintendo of America asked the team to reconvene and release the submarine demo as downloadable software for the Nintendo DSi. But as the game – soon to be titled Steel Diver – expanded from just one mode (the side-scrolling submarine exploration and combat that would form the bulk of the game’s missions) to three modes (including Periscope Strike, a first-person torpedo shooter from the perspective of a periscope, and Steel Commander, a top-down strategy game partially inspired by the Japanese-exclusive 1990 Game Boy game Kaisen Game: Radar Mission), the Steel Diver team – now composed of both Nintendo designers and the 11 members of Giles Goddard’s company Vitei – decided to expand their demo into a full retail release. This initially led to an identity crisis for director Takaya Imamura, who revealed to Iwata that he briefly, “thought it would be fine to set the game in a flashy, glittery world like – and I’m not kidding – a submarine version of Mario Kart.” Sugiyama quickly shut that idea down, and the game proceeded with more traditional aquatic environments.

Highly invested in the project was the legendary Shigeru Miyamoto, who held a key piece of information from the team: Though Steel Diver was developed for the DS, he thought that it would make an even better showcase for the company’s yet-to-be-revealed 3DS. But it wasn’t until very late into the development process that the Steel Diver team even learned of the existence of the new console, a decision Miyamoto explained in Iwata Asks: “I knew the game was perfect for the Nintendo 3DS system, but I was afraid that if we switched from the Nintendo DS system to the Nintendo 3DS system in the middle of development, the contents wouldn’t be thoroughly fine-tuned. So after the Nintendo DS version was about done, I said, ‘Let’s shift this over to the Nintendo 3DS system.’” According to Imamura, “[w]hen we heard that, we already had plans for debugging. Development was all but over.”

The process of adding an extra dimension to the game proved difficult at first, with Imamura telling Iwata, “We thought we could just switch it over and it would look stereoscopic, but when we did, we couldn’t see it. […] We were among the first to develop software for the Nintendo 3DS system, so a sufficient development kit didn’t exist at the time.” But then, “one day it suddenly started popping out,” Goddard said in that same Iwata Asks article. And it came at just the right time, Goddard added: “It started looking 3D about the day before our presentation. If it hadn’t, the whole thing might have ended.” Ultimately, Imamura felt that the game had found its correct home on the 3DS, even if the process could have been improved: “I’m really glad we changed it over to the Nintendo 3DS system. But I think it would have turned out even better if Miyamoto-san had told us sooner that he wanted to make it for the Nintendo 3DS system [laughs]!”

When the Wii launched in 2006, it came bundled with a number of pre-installed “channels” – or what we would likely just call apps today. Among those was the Mii Channel, an avatar-maker co-directed by Animal Crossing and Splatoon creator Hisashi Nogami. In an Iwata Asks interview, Nogami said that something like the Miis was an idea Miyamoto “had wanted to realize for some time.” Nogami revealed that originally the “plan was to develop three games in which the same characters designed by the player would appear.” But as development on the Wii advanced, the concept had “broadened to encompass the entire Wii.” Miis were integral features of the Wii’s user-interface, appearing in a large number of games including, most importantly, the Wii’s landmark pack-in, Wii Sports, and becoming a defining aspect of Nintendo’s cultural identity. In a 2008 fiscal report Q&A, Iwata made clear just how seriously the company viewed Miis as part of its brand, stating that, to “Nintendo, licensing Mii is identical to licensing Mario.” The Mii was now Nintendo, and it should be treated like its other icons.

However, it was not immediately clear to the general public whether the Mii was tied specifically to the Wii – with which it shared all but one letter – or if it would become Nintendo’s default avatar-creation system for the next two decades-plus, as we now know it has. Having launched in 2004, the DS did not include native Mii creation software, but it showed the first small signs that the Mii would become a core part of the larger Nintendo ecosystem.

First, the thrillingly titled DS exercise game Personal Trainer: Walking – released in 2008 in Japan and 2009 in America – tied players’ pedometer-tracked steps to Mii avatars, which could be imported over from the Wii’s Mii Channel. However, players who did not own a Wii could only choose Miis from a series of random presets; there was no way to create a custom Mii within the game itself. The first DS game to feature a full Mii creation suite was 2009’s Tomodachi Collection, a Japan-exclusive social simulation game that would receive a more widely released sequel on the 3DS in 2013/2014 (a third game will arrive later this year.) But only three other DS games featured Miis at all: Ide Yousuke’s Healthy Mahjong DSi, a Japan-exclusive downloadable mahjong game; Kuruma de DS, also exclusive to Japan, a GPS-connected title made in collaboration with Toyota and Honda that could only be used in select cars; and Final Fantasy Crystal Chronicles: Echoes of Time, which could feature a Mii-emblazoned item only if the player was connected to someone playing on a Wii.

It wasn’t until the 3DS that it became clear that Miis would truly migrate away from their home system. The 3DS was pre-installed with an avatar creation application called Mii Maker. One of the system’s novel features was “StreetPass,” a communication system that allowed players to exchange data with other nearby players. Its showcase app was StreetPass Mii Plaza, in which up to 10 Miis could congregate and compete in minigames. By the end of 2013, the 3DS even had its own version of Miiverse, the Mii-based social network that first appeared on the Wii U.

The surest sign that Miis were here for good was Pilotwings Resort. The 3DS launch title was the third – and final, for now – entry in the Miyamoto-created Pilotwings franchise of flight-simulation games. Each of the previous games had also served as North American launch titles for their respective systems, with each game functioning as a technical showcase for its system’s upgraded graphical capabilities. 1991’s Pilotwings utilized the Super Nintendo’s Mode 7 graphics to deliver groundbreaking “3D” visuals, while 1996’s Pilotwings 64 gave players the chance to explore the Nintendo 64’s more authentically three-dimensional spaces. Pilotwings Resort continued this trend, affording early 3DS adopters a massive playground to experiment with the system’s stereoscopic 3D visuals.

The earlier Pilotwings were not full of classic Nintendo iconography, but Pilotwings Resort represented a major aesthetic break: Every character in the game was a Mii. This aligned the game more closely with a different recent – and more recognizable – Nintendo series: Wii Sports. The action of Pilotwings Resort even takes place on Wuhu Island, the fictional tropical location where 2007’s Wii Fit and 2009’s Wii Sports Resort were also set.

The origins of the island, however, trace back even further. When Nintendo showcased the Wii to journalists in May 2006, Wii Sports contained an additional game that was cut from the final release: a flight simulator called Airplane, in which players soared above an unnamed island that bore a number of striking similarities to Wuhu. Interestingly, as detailed in a 2006 Eurogamer article, Nintendo reps were quick to downplay any connection between Wii Sports Airplane and the Pilotwings franchise, with Matthew Kumar writing, “It’s not a Pilotwings, they say, despite featuring a lovely, relaxing island which features small towns to buzz over, and tunnels to barnstorm. And, oh, you know, rings to fly through to get points.” Additionally, Kumar wrote, “It’s not entirely clear how this would fit into the Wii Sports range (or pack) or, despite what they say, if it is even intended to. But as a tech demo for that Pilotwings game they’re going to unveil at TGS or something, it’s brilliant and I’m gasping for more.” By the time Pilotwings Resort finally saw the light of day a half-decade later, the Wii Sports franchise – and its iconic Miis – had climbed so high up the hierarchy of Nintendo’s first-party franchises that IGN’s review of the game opened with, “Wii Sports Resort is back. Did you miss it?”

Miis appeared throughout the 3DS’s lifetime. They served as player icons for games like Super Mario 3D Land and Kid Icarus: Uprising, even starring in their own idiosyncratic games like Tomodachi Life and Miitopia. Miis would also be baked into future systems like the Wii U, the Switch, and the Switch 2. But it was Pilotwings Resort – along with Mii Plaza – that showed Nintendo had bigger and more serious aspirations for the Mii outside of the Wii.

When the original Game Boy launched in 1989, arriving in tow was an accessory called the Game Link Cable. It allowed players to connect directly to other Game Boy systems, enabling competitive multiplayer sessions in early hits like Tetris. Seven years later, with the release of the first Pokémon games, the Game Link Cable found a new calling, allowing players to not just compete, but also to swap their pocket monsters with other players in their communities. In her book Super Nintendo: How One Japanese Company Helped the World Have Fun, Keza MacDonald argues that this marked a turning point for Nintendo: “Pokémon Red and Pokémon Blue’s emphasis on trading and sharing represented an inspired reinvention of the Game Boy Link Cable: Game Freak took a piece of technology that had been used exclusively for competition and made it about communication, as well.”

That design principle – that games were about sharing and communication, too – reached its apotheosis with the 3DS’s StreetPass feature, which allowed the system to actively and, more interestingly, passively communicate with other nearby 3DSs via locally established, internet-free connections, even when the console was set to sleep mode. At launch, StreetPass was most prominently featured in the preinstalled Mii StreetPass Plaza app, which included the game Find Mii, an RPG in which players’ parties were filled with Miis taken from other 3DSs they had passed by. As producer Kouichi Kawamoto told Kotaku’s Stephen Totilo, Find Mii emerged “from our drive to make players feel like they accomplish something by using StreetPass”. It was an idle game powered by physical activity. In doing so, StreetPass’s communication had taken the sharing principles of the Game Link Cable in an entirely novel direction.

StreetPass was also implemented into Nintendogs + Cats, the best-selling of the 3DS’s first-party launch titles. While Pokémon players of yore had to establish a physical connection to see other players’ collections, StreetPass enabled Nintendogs players to passively interact with other owners and their pets. You could take your 3DS on a walk to an actual dog park, for example, and if there were any other 3DS owners in range, you would head home with a series of journal entries featuring their Miis, their pets, any messages they’d sent, and perhaps even a gift. These Miis and their pets would also soon begin to populate the game in other ways: You might run into them on a walk or even compete against them in dog shows. Nintendogs on DS featured a similar feature – Bark Mode – but it required more active participation from players; with StreetPass, community-building was now a low-effort exercise (often involving actual exercise).

StreetPass was central to Nintendo’s conception of the 3DS. In an Iwata Asks article, the eponymous Iwata said that the concept of the 3DS was, “Carry Around, Affect Each Other and Something New Every Day.” Nintendogs + Cats producer Hideki Konno further stated, “[W]hile it’s definitely okay to enjoy the game at home, I hope players will go out walking around with their Nintendo 3DS system as often as possible. There’s a lot for that purpose not just in Nintendogs + Cats, but built into the system itself”. StreetPass was exactly the kind of kooky invention upon which Nintendo made its name, and its legacy of encouraging players to explore the world lives on in mobile games like Pokémon Go.

The 3DS would soon find better games – and better sales – but its modest launch lineup contained plenty of insight. Steel Diver’s winding path towards release evidenced Nintendo’s unwavering commitment to its internal ideas – and its most legendary designer’s unconventional style of communication. Pilotwings Resort further established a core part of Nintendo’s brand identity, while Nintendogs + Cats showed that even the most straightforward of Nintendo sequels could still feature peculiar innovations. Stereoscopic 3D may not have been the future of gaming, but other elements of the 3DS have stayed with us forever.

#4093. Heartopia goes to the movies with its next event

Heartopia's Whale Island will soon host a new event that's all about the magic of cinema.

Heartopia’s next in-game event has been announced, and it’s one you may not have seen coming. Developer XD Games revealed Dreamlight Cinematics Festival, an upcoming limited-time event that celebrates cinema and movie-making.

Dreamlight Cinematics kicks off March 21, and will run through May 1, available across the game’s PC and mobile versions.

Dreamlight Cinematics Festival takes place on Whale Island. And, perhaps as an unofficial Oscars tie-in, it’s all about classic Hollywood filmmaking. Not only that, it also celebrates the aesthetics and industrial design of that era.

All around the game’s world, you’ll be able to find festival-themed collectables, which you can then use to unlock free Time-Limited Exhibition Passes.

If you log in during the event’s runtime, you’ll get the Car Cinema furniture set for free. This cosmetic bundle comes with chairs that are modelled after vintage vehicles, as well as poster display stands with unique movie making-themed decorations.

If you’re looking to spend some money, the Deluxe Festival Pack comes with a large Island Sunset Billboard, which you can place outside your home so everyone knows you spent that money. The same pack also comes with the Popcorn Movie Ticket chat bubble skin, and a 10% bonus to Festival Tokens when you sell stuff at the store.

Regardless of which pack you get, you’ll earn collection points for each, which puts you on the path to unlocking outfits like the Dreamlight Cinematics Festival-specific Modern Show Dandy and Modern Show Belle. There’s also a Cinematic Moments building material set launching with this event.

For now, we have the above reveal trailer to go on, which does offer some idea of what it’s going to look like in-game. Until things kick off on the weekend, you best arm yourself with some Heartopia codes.

The best and biggest discounts of all, as is typically the case, are for those who don’t have an active PS Plus subscription at all right now. The discounts also get bigger the higher up the tier list you go.

If you sign up to Essential by November 30, you can get 20% off the usual price of the lowest tier for 12 months, dropping the price from $79.99 to $63.99. That’s just $5.33 a month, so less than half the cost of rolling monthly payments.

Only 12-month subscriptions have been discounted for Black Friday across all three tiers.

Every game coming to Essential, Extra, and Premium and the dates you'll be able to play them for free.

Again, the higher the tier you commit to for the next 12 months, the bigger the discount you stand to get. Extra, which grants you access to an ever-changing library of PS4 and PS5 games on top of multiplayer access and monthly free games, is 25% off if you sign up this weekend, dropping the annual cost from $134.99 to $101.24.

Signing up for Premium gets you all of the above along with PS Portal cloud streaming capabilities and access to the Classics Catalog, among other things. PlayStation runs these PS Plus offers every year for Black Friday. That means there will be people out there whose discounted annual deals run out just in time for them to take advantage of the next one each year. If you always feel like you’re on the outside looking in when everyone else is paying less for PS Plus on Black Friday, maybe try to time it right in 2027 so that your subscription expires just in time for you to get Plus for less during next year’s inevitably similar sale.

#4091. Is Your DualSense Running Low Playing GTA VI?

Those of you playing Grand Theft Auto VI on the PlayStation 5 might have noticed that you’re having to charge your controller a lot more than usual, especially if you are using the more expensive DualSense Edge. You also might have noticed that GTA VI uses every feature on that controller to its fullest potential. These two facts are not unrelated!

Grand Theft Auto VI makes exceptional use of the DualSense’s haptic triggers, vibrations, and speaker. You might not even realize how much it’s doing until or unless you turn these features off and find that you kind of miss all the things the controller is doing with them. While they’re a great value-add, they absolutely come at a cost to your battery life on the controller.

Based on our tests, an average session with GTA lasts about 4 hours and 30 minutes on a fully-charged standard DualSense — in this case, an OEM model that came with the PlayStation 5 Pro. A DualSense Edge is even lower, with reports averaging out to around 3 hours and 40 minutes. On a different game, like Phantom Blade 0, the Dualsense will last upwards of double that amount. Times will vary for people depending on whether they replaced the battery themselves, what they’re doing in the game, how old their controller is, etc. But by and large, you’re not going to get a ton of hours if you’re planning to sit around and spend all Thanksgiving weekend playing the game, at least not without a USB-C cable nearby.

But this is all sort of a PSA not to worry if you’re ending every session at one bar on the PS5 battery icon. Your controller isn’t dying, it’s just exhausted traveling around Vice City.

#4090. All the hype has already made Crimson Desert one of the biggest launches on Steam this year

We're merely days away from the end of the first quarter of 2026, and Crimson Desert has come in clutch to join the list of big sellers.

Crimson Desert, the open-world action RPG off-shoot from Korean MMO Black Desert Online, has officially launched, nearly six years after it was initially revealed. The game has been building up a lot of momentum over the years, which recently coalesced to turn it into one of 2026’s most anticipated titles.

All of it has been leading up to this moment, and the game appears to have landed smoothly, though not without controversy, as has seemingly become part of its MO.

It has not been 24 hours since Crimson Desert launched on PC and consoles, and it’s already become a big hit. On Steam, one of two stores where the game can be purchased (the other being the Epic Games Store), the game shot to the top of the charts.

The action RPG continued to accumulate more and more players on Steam, peaking at a very respectable 239,045 concurrent players (via SteamDB). Though its success was very much expected, we perhaps didn’t predict its peak would be that high.

Indeed, Crimson Desert has been in Steam’s top 100 global sellers list for six weeks, jumping up six spots to become the number one seller this week just before it launched. As we get closer to the weekend, the numbers could climb even higher.

This peak concurrent puts Crimson Desert in the same league as several of the other major releases of the first quarter of 2026. The top spot continues to belong to Slay the Spire 2, which peaked at a staggering 574,638 concurrent players. It happened just days after the juggernaut Resident Evil Requiem achieved its own 344,214 peak concurrent, which was the year’s highest up until Slay the Spire 2’s release. All three are well ahead of Nioh 3’s 88,045 peak concurrent, and Marathon’s nearly identical peak of 88,337.

Crimson Desert has seen something of a mixed reception by critics. James gave it three stars in our review, saying it “lacks the connective sinew to be truly functional,” which is a common criticism shared by other outlets. Many also lamented the sheer number of systems fighting for player attention, its poorly explained mechanics, and counterintuitive controls.

On Steam, at least, players have similarly been divided, with the current Steam user rating sitting at Mixed, based on 8,728 reviews. Unsurprisingly, most of the negative reactions fall on the clunky controls and the game’s tendency to, as one Steam user put it, “so miserably tries to be everything at once, and fails to be anything at all.”

Kick some demon tail as Garcia Hotspur on one devil of a ride. The flames of hell will feel frigid compared to the hot-blooded Garcia on his quest to get his girl back from the Lord of the Underworld.

Shadow the Hedgehog is back with Classic and Modern Sonic in SONIC X SHADOW GENERATIONS, an all-new collection featuring two unique experiences!

METRO Exodus is an epic, story-driven first person shooter from 4A Games that blends deadly combat and stealth with exploration and survival horror in one of the most immersive game worlds ever created.

Yakuza 0 Director's Cut is the definitive edition of the critically acclaimed prequel to the Yakuza series. Fight like hell through Tokyo and Osaka entertainment districts as yakuza Kazuma Kiryu and cabaret club manager Goro Majima in an epic crime drama of intertwined fates that created legends.

MOUSE: P.I. For Hire is an action-packed first-person shooter that draws inspiration from the classic cartoons of the 1930s. Its black and white rubber hose visuals are drawn by hand, frame by frame, delivering a striking vintage aesthetic.

Fraser is the News Editor at Pure Xbox, where he spends his time reporting on the biggest stories in the world of Xbox and beyond.

#4088. The Top 10 Open World Games

There was a time when video games were largely linear affairs. You either moved up and down or from left to right in enclosed spaces. As technology evolved, so did the scope of digital worlds. Now players are regularly treated to expansive environments filled with quests, interesting characters, and horizons that stretch further with every console generation. These experiences consume dozens if not hundreds of hours and knowing which titles are worth the time investment has become crucial. To that end, we’ve assembled a list of 10 great modern open-world games available today to help make what can be a paralyzing decision a little easier.

Note that these are listed in release date order and don’t necessarily represent the best games of all time. Rather, this will be an ever-changing list of quality titles to arrive in recent years that you should go out of your way to get lost in.

Grand Theft Auto is arguably the blueprint for open worlds in video games, and its sixth entry is the series' peak. In a universe steeped in satire and cynicism, protagonists Jason and Lucia are instantly likable figures worth rooting for. Their love story is absolutely worth your time, but even if you made the decision to ignore it, you'd be overwhelmed by Leonida's exceedingly vast playground, ripe for exploration. When we say GTAVI's scope is staggering, we are partially talking about the literal size of the map, but we're mainly talking about its density; every corner is meticulously crafted with people to meet and places to rob. It's one of the most believable spaces in gaming history, bolstered by incredible graphics and populated with characters only a little more zany than you'd encounter in its real-life equivalent of Florida. Its dozens of cars feel great to drive, and its dozens of guns are a thrill to shoot, but if you decide to get really into birdwatching instead, that's fine by us. Grand Theft Auto VI is one of the best games of this generation – it's no surprise it made its way onto this top 10 list. | Our review

In an overly simplistic way, Ghost of Yōtei basically took everything that worked about Sucker Punch’s 2020 open world action game, Ghost of Tsushima, and improved it. Exploration, combat, visuals, and narrative are all major steps up from the previous game, which was already fantastic. Atsu’s journey of revenge, fighting and exploring her way through Ezo, is an always-compelling experience, not because it radically re-addresses or changes the mechanics that made Tsushima so great, but rather because they are carefully iterated on and improved in sometimes subtle ways. And as an open world game, it constantly excels at giving the player worthwhile distractions that all appear to the player naturally. You’re not bouncing between points on an overworld map – you’re literally following the wind where it takes you and always ending up somewhere amazing doing something incredible. | Our review

Kingdom Come: Deliverance II is one of the highest-rated open worlds on this list, and for good reason. If Grand Theft Auto VI is the best modern-day open world, and Cyberpunk 2077 the best future-set open-world game, then KCDII is easily the best medieval open-world game in some time. Eschewing the more fantastical likes of the medieval open-world format – which The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt excellently covers on this list – KCDII does all it can to remain grounded and true to the 15th Century Kingdom of Bohemia land it’s set in. You follow Henry, whom you’ll craft through your decisions and upgrade choices, on a journey of retribution, rebellion, and reflection, and you’ll meet an unforgettable cast of characters along the way. They are the grounding elements to an otherwise wide-open adventure that lets you craft a narrative only you can craft. However you invest your time in this massive, sprawling medieval landscape will be reflected in the Henry you play as and how the world responds around you – there’s no shortage of mischief and chivalry to get up to, and across its dozens of hours, you’ll be taken through one of the most rewarding open games you can play today.  | Our Review

FromSoftware proves its punishing yet satisfying style of action RPG absolutely works in an open-world format. Brimming with mystery and danger, Elden Ring allows players to make their own way, providing little guidance or hand-holding, making every discovery feel like a genuinely exciting and well-earned reward. Unlike traditional Souls games, slamming against a difficult boss isn’t the end of the line. You can simply explore elsewhere and fall down the rabbit holes of breaching an impregnable fortress, surviving a treacherous swamp, or taking down dozens upon dozens of other imposing enemies. Quality-of-life additions such as free fast travel and friendlier checkpointing before boss fights alleviate some stress, further encouraging you to hop aboard your spectral mount and uncover every secret of this incredible world. | Our Review

The greatest trick the Forza Horizon series pulls is fooling players into liking racing games by disguising them as open-world RPGs. The latest entry, Horizon 5, serves as the pinnacle of that Trojan Horse-style design. Set in a stunningly beautiful rendition of Mexico, players sit behind hundreds of vehicles to compete in a seemingly endless number of wild races. Whether you're speeding against other cars or a 747 airplane, the sheer variety of events and an over-the-top tone make Horizon more lighthearted compared to most pure racing sims. In addition to traditional races, you can enjoy Horizon 5's entertaining take on battle royale, a zombie-infection mode, and absurd story-driven scenarios (like driving a parade float). A staggering collection of unlockable cars, purchasable homes to store said vehicles, plus cosmetics and goofy dances for your avatar create powerful incentives to score the winner's purse. Best-in-class driving mechanics solidify Horizon 5's first-place standing | Our Review

Though Cyberpunk 2077’s launch was rough (and that’s putting it lightly), developer CD Projekt Red successfully righted the ship and then some. By fixing launch issues and woes, continuing to add meaningful (and free) content like new quests, Cyberpunk Edgerunners items, and more, the game literally got better each year. The team closed out the game with the incredible Phantom Liberty expansion, which adds a heaping dose of Idris Elba and spy-thriller action to Night City, ensuring any V who steps into this dystopian future has hours upon hours of open-world fun to enjoy. Speaking of Night City, it’s one of the most fully realized metropolitan playgrounds on this list. Police react to your actions in real time, as do citizens; futuristic cars and motorbikes await you to live out your Akira slide dreams; and countless weapons and upgrades will help you become the greatest cybernetic warrior gangster this side of the Pacifica. Between side content, the golden path, and the unlisted-but-worth-engaging-in hidden activities spread throughout Night City, you’d be hard-pressed to find a better dystopian open-world shooter than Cyberpunk 2077. | Our Review

Few studios craft worlds that feel as lifelike as Rockstar Games, and Red Dead Redemption 2 might be their crowning achievement. Every inch of this wild west drips with immaculate detail and feels like you’ve stepped into a time portal to the 1800s. Survival elements such as cooking, camping, and hunting allow players to role-play as a trail-worn gunslinger effectively – and it’s more fun than you’d expect. Emergent side missions mean a fascinating story or memorable stranger can pop up at a moment’s notice, and there’s plenty of diversity when it comes to the strange sights you’ll stumble upon. Tack on an incredible story led by a deeply compelling protagonist in outlaw Arthur Morgan, and Red Dead Redemption 2 rivals not only the greatest games but the classic westerns that inspired it. | Our Review

What makes Breath of the Wild magical is that it unclutters years of triple-A open-world design. Instead of littering Hyrule with icons telling you where to go, it allows players to forge their own paths. It only has one mandatory mission: destroy Ganon. Since you can do that right away, everything else is optional. Even the largest games force you to adhere to the path of a main linear narrative. In BOTW, one player’s approach to slaying Ganon can be totally different from another’s. Do you complete the four primary dungeons? Seek out the Master Sword? Build up your hearts? The beauty of it all: there’s no wrong answer.

Link can climb any surface, meaning that, provided you have the stamina, you can reach the summit of any mountain and concoct numerous paths to your destination. Hyrule also operates on realistic physics and principles for players to experiment with (i.e., all metal objects conduct electricity). It boasts hundreds of shrines with concise, entertaining puzzles and numerous mysteries, be they majestic dragons or an island that’s more than meets the eye. Breath of the Wild rocks for promoting improvisation and creativity more than anything. Its legacy has been cemented thanks to a growing number of titles borrowing from its playbook, such as Genshin Impact and Immortals Fenyx Rising. | Our Review

The Witcher 3’s gritty fantasy world is as beautiful as it is deadly. We would never want to actually live in it, though, due to its densely packed population of supernatural monsters, tyrannical rulers, and (typically) backstabbing citizens. The Witcher 3’s Continent keeps you on your toes thanks to the impact of its choice-driven gameplay. Small choices often come back around hours later in more significant ways than you expect, making every shifty thief, sultry mage, or cowardly would-be-knight worth engaging. With a compelling main storyline, dozens of meaningful sidequests, and boatloads of treasures, The Witcher 3, as well as its phenomenal expansions, succeeds in making its gargantuan setting worth uncovering. | Our Review

For lists about the best games on various platforms, check out our lists of the top 10 games on PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S, Switch 2, PlayStation 4, Xbox One, and Switch.

#4087. Splatoon 3 Version 12.0.1 Update Out Now, Here Are The Patch Notes

Last week, Nintendo released a major update for its team-based squid-shooter Splatoon 3, bumping the game up to Version 12.0.0.

It included changes to multiplayer, weapons adjustments, changes to Anarchy Battle, and even a change to the GameChat feature on Switch 2. Now, following this, Nintendo has released Version 12.0.1. The English patch notes aren't live just yet, but it is only a small update compared to the previous one.

According to a rough machine translation, it includes a fix for Anarchy Battle. Here's the rundown via Nintendo's Japanese website. We'll update this with the English patch notes when they go live.

Fixed an issue in Anarchy Battle (Series) where the matchmaking process would sometimes fail to complete.

*The latest update data is required to access online features. *Local wireless play is not compatible with versions prior to 12.0.0. Please ensure that all players you are playing with are using the same version of the update data. *Battle Replays are compatible with version 12.0.0, but are not compatible with versions 11.3.0 or earlier.

As usual, certain features such as local wireless and battle replays may not be compatible with earlier versions of the game.

You can find out more about what Splatoon 3 Version 12.0.0 included in our previous post here on Nintendo Life. In case you missed it, Splatoon Raiders recently got an eShop demo.

#4085. Crimson Desert's first patch aims at fixing controls, but it mostly affects mouse and keyboard

The first post-launch patch for Crimson Desert is here, and the list of changes is promising, even if it doesn't go far enough to address some deeper issues.

Crimson Desert has been out for a few days now, and as positive as its been received by many players, the game suffers from several fundamental issues that anyone who’s played it has called out.

Perhaps the loudest one of those has been how the game controls, which is a problem that stems from the complexity of controls themselves, as well as the underlying animations behind many of the actions the player character performs.

In the first case, at least, something is being done.

Developer Pearl Abyss rolled out patch 1.00.03 for Crimson Desert on Monday. The patch is available now on Steam and PlayStation, with Xbox and the Epic Games Store following “at a later time.”

Today’s update follows a letter to players the developer issued on Saturday. The letter generally acknowledged player feedback, but specifically pointed to complaints about the game’s clunky controls as something of a focus for the team.

The action RPG has actually broken its launch peak concurrent player numbers over the weekend, though only by a few thousands more. Its Steam user review rating has also improved over the same period.

This latest update only includes an initial set of fixes, but Pearl Abyss vowed to keep working on addressing all other points of feedback. A highlight in 1.00.03 is the addition of a Storage at Howling Hill Camp, which can be used to store inventory items.

The most important changes, of course, affect how the game controls on keyboard and mouse. Pearl Abyss included several fixes and altered some of the default presets to make the experience less painful when playing the game with a keyboard and mouse.

There are sadly no changes to controllers, but it is something that the developer said we can expect to see in future patches. More improvements for keyboard and mouse setups are in the works, too.

Beyond the control changes, patch 1.00.03 also includes a set of gameplay tweaks, especially when it comes to enemy health and difficulty. It also makes fast travelling more convenient, and brings a few fixes to NPC dialogue. You can read the full change log on Steam.

If you’re deep in Crimson Desert already, we definitely recommend giving our guides a look. We recently added new pages to help you figure out where to socket your Abyss Gear, how to find Contribution Points - and where to spend them, as well as more generally helpful information like how to expand your inventory, and how to reveal the map.
